entry: Hormone and medication, also called [[Epinephrine (medication)|epinephrine]]. It is normally produced by the [[Adrenal gland|adrenal glands]] and by a small number of neurons in the medulla oblongata. It plays an essential role in the [[Fight-or-flight response|fight-or-flight response]] by increasing blood flow to muscles, raising heart output, dilating the pupils and raising [[Blood sugar level|blood sugar level]]. It acts by binding to alpha and beta [[Receptor (biochemistry)|receptors]]. As a medication, it is used to treat [[Anaphylaxis|anaphylaxis]], [[Cardiac arrest|cardiac arrest]] and superficial bleeding; inhaled adrenaline may improve the symptoms of croup, and it may be used for [[Asthma|asthma]] when other treatments are not effective. It is also used to lower intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma by increasing the outflow of aqueous humor from the eye. Common side effects include shakiness, anxiety and sweating, and a fast heart rate and high blood pressure may occur.

[[Fixed-wing aircraft]] propelled forward by thrust from a jet engine, propeller or rocket engine. Airplanes serve in recreation, transportation of goods and people, military roles and research. Worldwide, commercial aviation carries more than four billion passengers a year on [[Airliner|airliners]]. Most are flown by a pilot on board, but some, such as drones, are remotely or computer-controlled. The [[Wright brothers]] flew the Wright Flyer in 1903, recognized as the first sustained and controlled heavier-than-air powered flight. They built on the work of [[George Cayley]], who set forth the concept of the modern airplane in 1799, and [[Otto Lilienthal]], whose 1891 flight attempts are seen as the beginning of human flight. The [[De Havilland Comet|de Havilland Comet]] was the first jet airliner, introduced in 1952; the [[Boeing 707]] was in commercial service from 1958 to 2019.

Slovak statesman and de facto leader of Czechoslovakia (1968–69). He oversaw reforms to the communist system during the [[Prague Spring]] and was best known for the slogan “[[Socialism]] with a human face.” Reforms were opposed by conservatives who benefited from the [[Stalinism|Stalinist]] economy and by Soviet-bloc interests. On the night of 20–21 August 1968, half a million [[Warsaw Pact]] troops invaded Czechoslovakia; the invasion was intended to enable a coup by conservative forces, but the coup could not materialize because of the popularity of Dubček and the reformist leadership. Dubček was forced to resign as party head in April 1969. During the [[Velvet Revolution]] in 1989 he chaired the federal parliament and contended for the presidency with [[Václav Havel]]. The [[European Parliament]] awarded him the Sakharov Prize that year, and [[Andrei Sakharov]] credited him and the Prague Spring as his inspiration.

English children's novel by [[Lewis Carroll]], published in 1865. A little girl named Alice falls through a rabbit hole into a [[Fantasy|fantasy]] world of anthropomorphic creatures, and the book is seen as an example of literary nonsense. It has become one of the best-known works of Victorian literature and is credited with helping to end an era of didacticism in [[Children's literature|children's literature]]. The artist [[John Tenniel]] provided 42 wood-engraved illustrations for the original edition. The novel has never been out of print and has been translated into 174 languages. Its legacy includes adaptations to screen, radio, ballet, opera and [[Musical theatre|musical theatre]], as well as theme parks, board games and video games. Carroll published a sequel, *Through the Looking-Glass*, in 1871.

American television sitcom broadcast on [[CBS]], 1971–79. Produced by [[Norman Lear]] and based on the British series *Till Death Us Do Part*, it centers on a working-class family in [[Queens]], New York, led by the prejudiced Archie Bunker, played by [[Carroll O'Connor]]. The series is arguably one of American television's most influential comedies, and it topped the Nielsen ratings from 1971 to 1976, the first series to hold that position for five consecutive years.

Natural history museum on the Upper West Side of [[Manhattan]], [[New York City]]. The museum complex comprises 21 interconnected buildings with 45 permanent exhibition halls, a planetarium and a library. Its collections contain about 32 million specimens and artifacts, of which only a small fraction can be displayed at any time. It is a private 501(c)(3) organization with a full-time scientific staff of 225, and it sponsors over 120 special field expeditions each year. Naturalist Albert S. Bickmore devised the idea for the museum in 1861, and it opened within [[Central Park|Central Park]]'s Arsenal on May 22, 1871. Its first purpose-built structure in Theodore Roosevelt Park, across from Central Park, opened in 1877. In 2020 the equestrian statue of [[Theodore Roosevelt]] was removed after protests, and in 2021 the museum acknowledged its historical ties to eugenics research.

Set of building styles of [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]], spanning more than three thousand years. Religious and funerary architecture, the great majority of what survives, was generally conservative in taste. The best-known examples are the [[Pyramid|pyramids]] and the [[Sphinx]]. Most buildings were made of locally available mud brick and limestone, and stone was reserved mainly for tombs and temples. Walls, columns and piers were covered with hieroglyphic and pictorial carvings painted in brilliant colors, and many motifs, such as the scarab and the vulture, are symbolic. Monumental buildings used post-and-lintel construction, and [[Column|columns]] typically had capitals decorated to resemble plants such as the [[Papyrus|papyrus]]. The [[Pyramid of Djoser|Step Pyramid of Djoser]] at [[Saqqara]] was designed by [[Imhotep]]. Egyptian motifs influenced architecture elsewhere, reaching the wider world during the Greek Orientalizing period and again in the nineteenth-century Egyptomania.

Russian and Soviet poet, pen name of Anna Andreyevna Gorenko. She began writing poetry at age 11, inspired by [[Alexander Pushkin]], [[Jean Racine]] and [[Nikolay Nekrasov]]. Her work ranges from short lyric poems to intricately structured cycles, and its economy and emotional restraint were strikingly original to her contemporaries. Her early work (1912–25) was followed by later work from around 1936 until her death, divided by a decade of reduced literary output. Her work was condemned and censored by [[Stalinism|Stalinist]] authorities, and she chose to remain in the [[Soviet Union]] rather than emigrate. Her cycle *Requiem* (1935–40) addresses the Stalinist terror, and her first husband, [[Nikolai Gumilev]], was executed by the Cheka. Her son and her common-law husband Nikolay Punin spent many years in the [[Gulag]], where Punin died.

Brazilian composer, pianist, guitarist and songwriter, known as Tom Jobim. He is considered one of the fathers of [[Bossa nova|bossa nova]], a style that merged [[Samba|samba]] with cool [[Jazz|jazz]] in the 1960s, and he is regarded as one of the most celebrated songwriters of the 20th century. His song “[[The Girl from Ipanema]]” has been recorded more than 240 times by other artists and is believed to be one of the most recorded popular songs in history. Several of his compositions appear on the 1964 album *Getz/Gilberto*, which won [[Grammy Awards]] and was the first jazz record to win Album of the Year, and in 1967 he recorded an album with [[Frank Sinatra]]. Born in the Tijuca district of [[Rio de Janeiro]], he earned his living in nightclubs and bars before starting to achieve success as a composer.

Set of multiple connected [[Antenna (radio)|antennas]] that work together as a single antenna to transmit or receive [[Radio wave|radio waves]]. Its elements are fed with a specific [[Phase (waves)|phase]] relationship, so that signals reinforce in desired directions and cancel in others. Using more elements gives higher gain and a narrower beam, and some military phased array [[Radar|radars]] are composed of thousands of individual antennas. Arrays are also used for radio direction finding and in [[Radio astronomy|radio astronomy]] for high-resolution imaging.

Dutch astronomer, historian and Marxist theorist. He studied mathematics and physics at [[Leiden University]] and wrote his thesis on the variability of [[Algol]]. He also researched the [[Milky Way]] and the variability of [[Polaris]]. He became a convinced [[Socialism|socialist]] and was one of the main theorists of council communism. After he was reprimanded for leading a strike support committee, the Dutch government dismissed him from the Leiden Observatory, and in 1918 the Amsterdam city council appointed him as a lecturer at the [[University of Amsterdam]].

Willful killing of a prominent or important person by sudden or secret attack, typically for political, social or ideological reasons. Assassinations may be ordered by individuals or organizations and carried out by themselves or hired accomplices, and they have been performed since ancient times. Victims have included [[Philip II of Macedon]] and Roman dictator [[Julius Caesar]], and seven Persian kings of the Achaemenid dynasty were murdered between 550 BC and 330 BC. The word assassin is believed to derive from hashshashin, a term for members of the [[Order of Assassins]], a Nizari Ismaili group active in the Near East from the 11th to 13th centuries; the association with hashish is debated. The verb appears in [[Medieval Latin]] from the mid-13th century, and it was first used in printed English in 1600, five years before [[William Shakespeare]] used it in *Macbeth*.

Period of [[History of Japan|Japanese history]], 538–710. Named after the Asuka region in present-day [[Nara Prefecture]], it saw the introduction of [[Buddhism]] and the adoption of [[China|Chinese]] writing. It is the first time in Japanese history that the emperor ruled relatively uncontested, and the name of the country changed from Wa to Nippon. The term was proposed around 1900 by fine-arts scholars Sekino Tadasu and [[Okakura Kakuzō]]; historians generally follow Okakura, who ended it with the transfer of the capital to Nara rather than with Sekino’s [[Taika Reform]] of 646.

Punjabi Muslim mystic, poet and preacher. Revered by Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs alike, he was educated at [[Multan]] and [[Delhi]], and after his master died he returned to Punjab and settled in Ajodhan, present-day Pakpattan, [[Pakistan]]. He is counted among the founders of the Chishti Sufi order. It is uncertain whether the verses attributed to him in the [[Guru Granth Sahib]] are his, as one scholar argues, their language more closely resembles a later stage of Punjabi.

Two-player [[Board game|board game]] played with counters and [[Dice|dice]]. Each player has 15 pieces, known traditionally as men and in the United States as [[Checkers|checkers]], that move along 24 points according to the roll of two dice. The first player to bear off all 15 pieces wins, and removing them while the opponent is still far behind is a triple win known as a backgammon. Backgammon combines strategy and luck, and an optional doubling cube lets players raise the stakes. It is a [[Race game|race game]] in the large family of tables games, whose ancestors date back at least 1,600 years. The Persian game of nard was linked by one text to [[Ardashir I]], and the [[Royal Game of Ur]] from 2600 BC may be an ancestor. The earliest specific reference to backgammon is a letter from 1647, when it was emerging in England.

Series of Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms on the volcanic island of [[Bali]], in the [[Lesser Sunda Islands]], Indonesia. Their history was closely tied to [[Java]], and after the fall of [[Majapahit]] in the late 15th century Hindu courtiers and artisans took refuge on Bali. From the mid-19th century the [[Dutch East Indies]] campaigned against the minor kingdoms, and by the early 20th century it had conquered them, some after *puputan* fights that ended in mass ritual suicide, ending a millennium of native independent rule.

Capital city of [[West Java]] province, Indonesia. It lies in a river basin surrounded by volcanic mountains, a natural defense that was the main reason the [[Dutch East Indies]] government planned to move the capital from Batavia, now [[Jakarta]]. The Dutch established tea plantations in the mountains in the 18th century, and in the early 20th century the city became an exclusive resort for Europeans, earning the nickname *Parijs van Java*. The Bandung Conference, the first Asian-African Conference, was hosted by President [[Sukarno]] in 1955 and is now held every ten years. Bandung joined the [[UNESCO]] Creative Cities Network in 2015, and in 2017 it won a regional award for having the cleanest air among major ASEAN cities. It is Indonesia's major technology centre.

Irish stage, film and television actor, born William Joseph Shields. He joined the Abbey Theatre in [[Dublin]] in 1915 and played Captain Jack Boyle in the premiere of [[Seán O'Casey]]'s *Juno and the Paycock* in 1924. He won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *Going My Way* (1944), and was nominated for Best Actor for the same performance. He is also known for Hollywood films directed by [[John Ford]].

State in northeastern [[Nigeria]], with the city of [[Bauchi (city)|Bauchi]] as its capital. Formed in 1976, it is the fifth largest of Nigeria's 36 states in area and the fifth most populous, with an estimated population of over 8,308,800 in 2022. Its landscape includes Yankari National Park, home to large populations of waterbuck, [[African buffalo]], [[Hippopotamus|hippopotamus]] and some of Nigeria's last remaining lions. Agriculture is central to the economy, and [[Tin|tin]] and columbite mining are also important. In the early 1800s the Bauchi Emirate was formed under the [[Sokoto Caliphate]].

King of Italy (r. 887–924) and Holy Roman Emperor (r. 915–924). He is usually known as Berengar of Friuli, having ruled the March of Friuli from 874, and he was elected to replace [[Charles the Fat]] in Italy after that ruler’s deposition in 887. His long reign of 36 years was opposed by seven other claimants to the Italian throne and is usually characterized as troubled. After his death an imperial [[Interregnum]] lasted 38 years, until the German king Otto I was crowned emperor in 962.

Brazilian [[Volleyball|volleyball]] coach and former player, known as Bernardinho. He was head coach of the Brazilian men's team when it won Olympic gold at the 2004 [[Athens]] Games and the 2016 Rio Olympics, and of the women's team that won bronze at the 1996 Atlanta and 2000 [[Sydney]] Olympics. With 48 medals overall, he is the most successful team sport coach of all time, as of 2021.

Ranged weapon system of an elastic launching device, the bow, and long-shafted [[Projectile|projectiles]], the [[Arrow|arrows]]. Humans used bows and arrows for [[Hunting|hunting]] and aggression long before recorded history, and they were important weapons of war until [[Firearm|firearms]] made them increasingly obsolete in the early modern period. Today they are mostly used for hunting and sports. When drawn, the bow's limbs act as cantilever springs that store elastic energy, which is released through the [[Bowstring|bowstring]] to propel the arrow. The oldest known evidence of arrows comes from the Obi-Rakhmat Grotto in [[Uzbekistan]], some 80,000 years ago. After the end of the [[Last Glacial Period|last glacial period]], the bow spread to nearly every inhabited region except Australasia and most of Oceania.

Extensive geographical region covering most of eastern, southern and central [[Brazil]]. It covers some 4,500,000 sq km, about half of the country's land area, and the vast majority of Brazil's population lives in the highlands or on the adjacent coastal strip. Ancient [[Basalt|basaltic]] lava flows formed much of the region, but no seismic or volcanic activity remains. [[Erosion]] has also shaped the highlands, forming extensive sedimentary deposits and wearing down the mountains. The region is usually divided into the Atlantic Plateau, once almost completely covered by the [[Atlantic Forest]] (of which only 7.3% remains); the Southern Plateau; and the Central Plateau, about 85% of which was once covered by [[Cerrado|Cerrado]] vegetation. Several mountain ranges, including the [[Serra do Mar]], are considered part of the highlands.

Widespread species of [[Rat|rat]], *Rattus norvegicus*. Despite the name Norway rat, it is thought to have originated in northern [[China]] and neighboring areas. It has spread to all continents except [[Antarctica]] and is the dominant rat in [[Europe]] and much of [[North America]]. One of the largest muroids, it weighs 140–500 g and has a body length of up to 28 cm. With rare exceptions, it lives wherever humans live, particularly in urban areas, and it is omnivorous, reproduces rapidly and can be a vector for several human diseases. [[Selective breeding]] has produced the fancy rat and the [[Laboratory rat|laboratory rat]], both of the domesticated subspecies *Rattus norvegicus domestica*. Studies of wild rats in New York City have shown that populations in different neighborhoods can evolve distinct genomic profiles.

Family of large terrestrial [[Bird|birds]], including floricans and korhaans. Most inhabit dry grassland and [[Steppe|steppe]] regions. Bustards range from 40 to 150 cm in length and are omnivorous and opportunistic, eating leaves, seeds, fruit, small vertebrates and invertebrates. The kori bustard and the great bustard are frequently cited as the world's heaviest flying birds. In most bustards the males are substantially larger than the females, and the group is among the most [[Sexual dimorphism|sexually dimorphic]] of birds. There are 26 recognized species. The common name derives from the Latin *avis tarda*, given by [[Pliny the Elder]], and tarda means slow and deliberate, an apt description of the bird's walk. The family name Otididae derives from the genus Otis, which [[Carl Linnaeus]] gave to the great bustard in 1758.
